selfCorrection.summary: GHN-V2-B1 is a blocker I not only missed but affirmatively endorsed, and it is the direct sequel to a discipline I had recorded one review earlier. I returned ACCEPT on v2 at 0 blockers and 0 advisories.
selfCorrection.theDefect: v2 renamed requiredNow to requiredNowCountable and set it to sixteen, removing DR-G03 and DR-G04 from the required set alongside DR-G17. Those two removals do not rest on the same authority. D-077 removes G17 because the SARIF ride dropped, so the gate is inapplicable — the requirement itself is gone. D-006 does not do that for G03/G04: it makes a valid name contingent on machine pins and product sign-off, which blocks the naming act while leaving the gate required. v2 applied one subtraction rule to two different situations, and the result was a 'sixteen of sixteen' target that reads as complete while two required gates stand unnamed.
selfCorrection.howIEndorsedIt: My v2 verdict says I 'verified the arithmetic two independent ways and both give sixteen', and specifically that 'the countable sixteen is precisely D-002's required nineteen with G03, G04 and G17 removed: I expanded D-002's list independently and the resulting set matches requiredNowCountable element for element.' That is true as arithmetic and irrelevant as validation. I confirmed the subtraction was performed correctly without asking whether each subtrahend had authority to be subtracted.
selfCorrection.whyThisIsWorseThanTheEarlierMisses: One review earlier I recorded a discipline in these exact terms: a disclosed dependency still has arithmetic consequences, test disclosures against counts. I then applied it to the numerator — catching that G03/G04 must not count as named — and did not apply it to the denominator, where the same disclosure means they must still count as required. In the same v2 verdict I quoted with approval the sentence 'Condition 4 would still not be MET: G03/G04 machine pins remain', and endorsed a sixteen-of-sixteen target in the next breath. Two required gates unnamed and a denominator that reads complete, side by side in a document I called exact.
selfCorrection.theSecondFinding: GHN-V2-A1, the G13 ambiguity, is milder and also mine to have raised. In reviewing v2 I ran a query and reported 'gates flagged contributes=False: DR-G03, DR-G04, DR-G17', while separately recording that G13 was blocked on DR-118. I printed a list that omitted a gate I knew was blocked and did not ask why. v2's G13 carried namingStanding NAMED-NOT-AUTHORED, identical to fully named gates, so it was readable as currently named.
selfCorrection.refinedDiscipline: Two rules, both sharper than the one they replace. First: when an item leaves a set, check the authority for the removal and what that authority actually removes — blocking an act is not the same as removing the requirement the act would satisfy, and arithmetic correctness of a subtraction says nothing about its legitimacy. Second: read a denominator with the same suspicion as a numerator. A shrinking denominator flatters progress exactly as an inflated numerator does, and it is the less visible of the two because the number that moves is the one nobody is looking at.

acceptNote: ACCEPT at 0 blockers and 0 advisories. The repair puts the eighteen back and keeps the sixteen only as a labelled progress category, then defends the distinction three ways — a note saying it is not a replacement required-set, a countCheck ending 'never 16 of 16', and an instruction that the later MF-6 write must not present 16 as the denominator. I checked the arithmetic in four independent relations and all four close. My self-correction is recorded in full because this one is not a near-miss: I read v2's admission that two required gates remained unnamed, quoted it approvingly, and in the same verdict endorsed a denominator that made the target complete without them. The lesson I am taking is that a subtraction being arithmetically correct says nothing about whether the authority cited had power to make it, and that a denominator deserves the same suspicion as a numerator because it is the number nobody is watching.
